opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the geometry is actually the part I find most beautiful about it.

The starting point is a simple fact we proved: a linear classifier can't do better than a constant predictor at recovering a concept from a representation if and only if the class-conditional means are all the same. Equivalently, the cross-covariance between the representation X and the one-hot concept label Z is zero. So "linear guardedness" reduces to a statement about first moments. You don't need to reason about every possible linear probe; you just need to zero out that cross-covariance.

The natural first idea is an orthogonal projection: find the subspace spanned by the cross-covariance and project it out. That does remove linear information, but it isn't minimal. It can distort the representation more than necessary, because the representation isn't isotropic. Some directions have huge variance, some very little, and they're correlated.

So the trick in LEACE is to work in a whitened coordinate system. You apply the inverse square root of the covariance of X, which makes the data isotropic, so Euclidean distance there corresponds to Mahalanobis distance in the original space. In that whitened space you do an ordinary orthogonal projection onto the complement of the column space of the whitened cross-covariance. Then you unwhiten to get back.

Composed together, that gives an *oblique* projection in the original space. It isn't orthogonal in the usual sense, but it's the projection that removes exactly the linearly available concept information while changing the representation as little as possible in expected squared distance. And the least-squares optimality holds under a broad family of norms, not just one particular choice. You add back the mean shift so it's affine, and you get a closed-form eraser that's provably optimal. No adversarial training, no iterative procedures like INLP that keep peeling off directions and often remove far more than they need to.

One way I like to put it: the eraser collapses the concept along precisely the directions that carry it, measured in the geometry the data itself defines, and leaves everything else untouched. The rank of the edit is at most the number of classes minus one, so for a binary concept you're making a rank-one change.

Of course, there's a caveat. That guarantee is about *linear* information. Nonlinear probes can sometimes still recover the concept, because you've matched the means but not, say, the covariances. That's part of what pushed us to think about quadratic erasure and the deeper question of what it really means for information to be "removed" from a network.

r001.rationale: It says whitening makes the data isotropic, meaning variance is equal across directions.

r002.rationale: It describes projection onto the complement of the whitened cross-covariance’s column space, but does not describe a hyperplane normal to the difference between two class centroids.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says to unwhiten after projecting in whitened space.

r004.rationale: It connects zero cross-covariance with equal class-conditional means and later says the guarantee follows because the means are matched.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I like to think about it is that LEACE is fundamentally a statement about what "erasing a concept" even means geometrically, and once you pin that down the method sort of falls out.

So the setup is: you have some representation space, say the residual stream of a transformer, and you have a concept, like gender or part of speech, that takes on some finite set of values. And you want to edit the representations so that no linear classifier can recover that concept anymore. Not just a particular probe you trained, but any linear probe at all.

The key insight, and this is really the whole thing, is that linear guardedness is equivalent to a very simple condition: the class-conditional means have to coincide. If the mean representation for "male" and the mean for "female" are the same point, then there's no linear direction along which the classes separate in expectation, and you can prove no linear classifier beats chance. Conversely, if the means differ at all, a classifier can just project onto the difference and do better than chance. So the question "what does a linear concept look like geometrically" has a surprisingly clean answer: it lives in the span of the differences between class means. That's a subspace of dimension at most k minus one for k classes.

Once you see that, the erasure problem becomes: find the minimal edit to the representations that collapses those class means onto each other. And "minimal" is where the geometry gets interesting. You don't want to just naively project out the raw mean-difference directions, because the representation space isn't isotropic. Some directions have huge variance and some have almost none, and the features are correlated. So LEACE works in the whitened space. You take the covariance of the representations, whiten everything so that the geometry is actually Euclidean in the sense that matters for the data, do an orthogonal projection there that removes the component correlated with the concept, and then un-whiten. The result is an oblique projection in the original coordinates.

And you can prove this is optimal: among all affine maps that achieve linear guardedness, LEACE is the one that moves the representations the least in expected squared distance. So you're not just erasing the concept, you're doing the least collateral damage to everything else encoded in the space. The earlier methods, like INLP, were iterative and would keep peeling off directions and end up carving out way more of the space than necessary. LEACE is closed-form and surgical in comparison.

The thing I find kind of beautiful is that it's really just a cross-covariance argument. The whole method reduces to the cross-covariance between your representations and the one-hot concept labels. Zero that out, with the right metric, and you're done. There's no training, no adversarial game, it's just linear algebra on second moments.

Now, the caveat I always want to flag is that this is specifically about linear information. Nonlinear probes can sometimes still recover the concept, because the class-conditional distributions can have identical means and still differ in their higher moments. So LEACE is a precise tool for a precise notion of erasure, and I think it's important not to oversell it as making a concept disappear in some absolute sense. But for a lot of what people actually want, like understanding how much a model's behavior relies on linearly accessible features, or doing fair downstream classification, that linear notion is exactly the right one.

r001.rationale: It says whitening makes the geometry Euclidean, but does not state that representation variance becomes equal in every direction.

r002.rationale: It describes an orthogonal projection in whitened space, but does not specify projection onto a hyperplane normal to the difference between two class centroids.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says to un-whiten after the projection.

r004.rationale: It says the edit collapses the class means onto each other.

astra-6.text:
I think the cleanest geometric picture is: whiten the representation, project out the directions associated with the concept, and then undo the whitening.

Whitening matters because the representation can have very different amounts of variance in different directions. In whitened coordinates, we can identify the subspace that carries linear information about the concept and remove it with an orthogonal projection. When you map that operation back into the original coordinates, it’s generally an oblique projection—the direction you move a point isn’t necessarily perpendicular to the subspace you’re projecting onto.

That’s a useful distinction from simply finding a linear probe and projecting out its weight vector. The probe’s weights describe how to read information out; they don’t necessarily tell you the best direction in which to change the representation to erase that information.

LEACE chooses an affine transformation that eliminates the cross-covariance with the concept while minimizing mean squared change to the representation. For a categorical concept, you can think of the constraint as making the class means coincide. That gives you the linear erasure guarantee, but it doesn’t mean the entire class distributions become identical. Nonlinear information can still remain.

r001.rationale: The response says whitening addresses differing variance, but does not state that it makes variance equal in every direction.

r002.rationale: It describes an orthogonal projection in whitened coordinates, but does not specify a hyperplane normal to the difference between two class centroids.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says to undo the whitening after projecting.

r004.rationale: It says that for a categorical concept the constraint can be viewed as making the class means coincide.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that we want to remove the directions that carry linear information about a concept, while changing the representation as little as possible. And those two requirements don’t generally mean just taking an orthogonal projection in the original space.

Imagine your representations form this elongated cloud. If you project out a direction using ordinary Euclidean geometry, you can throw away a lot of variation that you didn’t need to remove. So, conceptually, LEACE first whitens the representations, making the covariance spherical. In that space, you project out the subspace correlated with the concept, and then you undo the whitening.

The resulting transformation is generally an oblique projection in the original coordinates. That’s the interesting geometric bit: the directions you remove and the subspace you project onto don’t have to be perpendicular. That extra flexibility lets you eliminate the linear signal with minimum mean-squared distortion.

And the qualification is that this is linear concept erasure. You’ve removed the information available to a linear predictor; you haven’t necessarily made the concept impossible for a nonlinear predictor to recover.

r001.rationale: It says whitening makes the covariance spherical, which means representation variance is equal in every direction.

r002.rationale: It mentions projecting out a concept-correlated subspace in whitened space, but does not describe an orthogonal projection onto a hyperplane normal to the class-centroid difference.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says to undo the whitening after projecting.

r004.rationale: It says the linear signal is eliminated, but does not state that the class means coincide.
